doc.title: Genevieve Rose interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 14, 1998

chapter: Bass history, future and the scene
title: Pre-amplifier bass and band volume
summary: Rose explains early bands played softer so the bass could be heard, unlike loud modern ensembles.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I’m kind of always fascinated, when you think of the bass players in kind of the pre amplifier days, how they were expected to drive the part of the rhythm, to drive like a big band. And how were they heard?

Well I think one of the big things that a lot of people may forget about is that back then the bands didn’t play as loud, so they would only play as loud as they could hear the bass player. So even though the bass player had high action string, really loud, that style of playing, the bands weren’t all that quadruple forte that they play now. They were a lot softer, so you could hear the softer instruments. They didn’t cover up the sound of the bass. So I mean every once in a while I’ll still rehearse with the string bass acoustically with a big band, but it’s not the same because a lot of the time they’re just playing as if

you had an amplified bass. The horn players are blaring out and the drum is just as loud, and that’s why it doesn’t work a lot of time, having an unamplified bass, because the other musicians forget, like they have to play softer like they used to back in the 20s and 30s and 40s.
And when they were backing up singers too.
The singers had to hear themselves.
Right, yeah. And recording. If everybody played softer the levels were down farther.
I think society in general is louder.
Possibly, yeah. Definitely. Well Latin music is definitely loud.
